extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, historians, and policymakers studying crowd psychology and political influence
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Gustave Le Bon's principles on how crowds form beliefs and are influenced — including the remote and immediate factors shaping opinions and the 'religious' character of crowd convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressing the imagination of crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever strikes the imagination of crowds presents itself under the shape of a startling and very clear image, freed from all accessory explanation, or merely having as accompaniment a few marvellous or mysterious facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To influence crowds present condensed, startling, easily visualized images (a great victory, miracle, crime, or hope). Avoid explaining genesis or offering complex reasoning; a single striking event will impress more than many small facts or statistics (e.g., a visible public disaster impresses more than weekly mortality statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on reasoned demonstration to sway crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: The feat is never to be achieved by attempting to work upon the intelligence or reasoning faculty, that is to say, by way of demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional and symbolic acts (Antony reading Caesar's will and pointing to his corpse) are far more effective than rhetorical argument or logical demonstration when seeking to move a crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and immediacy trump statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not, then, the facts in themselves that strike the popular imagination, but the way in which they take place and are brought under notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make events visible, immediate, and singular rather than dispersed or abstract; statistical information rarely produces the same emotional impact as a concentrated, observable incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convictions of crowds take a religious shape
rubrics_metrics.description: When convictions are closely examined ... they always assume a peculiar form which I cannot better define than by giving it the name of a religious sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd beliefs—whether about a divinity, idol, hero, or political conception—share characteristics of religion (worship, submission, intolerance). Treat political or ideological appeals as potentially religious in form and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the religious sentiment in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: This sentiment has very simple characteristics, such as worship of a being supposed superior, fear of the power with which the being is credited, blind submission to its commands, inability to discuss its dogmas, the desire to spread them, and a tendency to consider as enemies all by whom they are not accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect fanaticism, intolerance, and an absence of critical discussion when a crowd adopts a belief; leaders and movements gain firmness when they inspire these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy becomes adoration; antipathy becomes hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: They only entertain violent and extreme sentiments, that in their case sympathy quickly becomes adoration, and antipathy almost as soon as it is aroused is transformed into hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small shifts in sentiment can escalate rapidly in crowds; careful management of emotional cues is crucial because positive/negative feelings polarize fast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success of founders depends on inspiring fanatical sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: All founders of religious or political creeds have established them solely because they were successful in inspiring crowds with those fanatical sentiments which have as result that men find their happiness in worship and obedience and are ready to lay down their lives for their idol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movements grow when leaders convert causes into objects of worship/obedience; propaganda should aim at inspiring devotion rather than solely rational assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factor: Race (predominant influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Race ... far surpasses in importance all the others. It represents the suggestions of ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/ethnic inheritance conditions what ideas a crowd can readily adopt; environmental stimuli contrary to racial suggestions are often only momentarily effective. Tailor appeals to the inherited character of a people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factor: Traditions as a synthesis of the race
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions represent the ideas, the needs, and the sentiments of the past. They are the synthesis of the race, and weigh upon us with immense force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditions are conservative and especially powerful within crowds; attempts to abolish deep-rooted customs are likely to fail or be reversed. Change is best accomplished gradually to balance stability and variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factor: Time prepares and destroys beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: It is time that prepares the opinions and beliefs of crowds, or at least the soil on which they will germinate. ... It is time that has prepared their blooming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beliefs require historical accumulation to take root; allow time for social transformations rather than expecting immediate effects from reforms or propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factor: Institutions are effects, not causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and social institutions ... are the outcome of ideas, sentiments, and customs, and that ideas, sentiments, and customs are not to be recast by recasting legislative codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions reflect national character/race and cannot by themselves change the genius of the masses; changing names or legal forms without addressing deeper social character yields superficial results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factor: Instruction and education have limited moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction neither renders a man more moral nor happier, that it changes neither his instincts nor his hereditary passions, and that at times--for this to happen it need only be badly directed--it is much more pernicious than useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware systems of education based on rote memorization (the 'Latin' system) which may produce obedience without judgment and can even increase social ills; well-directed practical instruction can improve professional capacity, but education alone is not a panacea for moral or social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate factors trigger collective action
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate factors ... serve as the source of active persuasion on crowds; that is, they are the factors which cause the idea to take shape and set it loose with all its consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches, dramatic incidents, and timely provocations operate on a prepared public to produce riots, strikes, or mass political decisions. Successful agitation combines remote preparation (race, tradition, time) with decisive immediate triggers (oratory, visible events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds do not reason; they accept or reject wholes
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds do not reason, that they accept or reject ideas as a whole, that they tolerate neither discussion nor contradiction, and that the suggestions brought to bear on them invade the entire field of their understanding and tend at once to transform themselves into acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication with crowds should focus on simple, whole-form messages and avoid complexity or internal contradiction; expect intolerance for dissent and rapid translation of ideas into action.
